title: Reforming the Judiciary -- Ch. 3: Battling Corruption, Incompetence and Delay
keywords: Juveniles in Conflict with the Law
primary_topics: Chapter 3 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- CJP's speech before 'this elite group representing American business in our country' explaining the Supreme Court's Action Program for Judicial Reform (APJR, 2001-2006) as the Court's answer to what he calls the 'CID' plagues: corruption, incompetence and delay

A diagnosis of the three problems: corruption beyond direct bribery, including 'the three "ships" that plague public service: friendship, relationship and kinship'; incompetence in judges and lawyers whose language and elementary law appall; and delay from antiquated procedures, rising caseloads, vacant judgeships and the abuse of rules

The Court's answers, sector by sector: unprecedented internal discipline (about 350 judges penalized in three years, and firsts against its own member, a CA justice and the Sandiganbayan presiding magistrate); fiscal autonomy and competitive pay to attract the best; continuing judicial education through Philja; the Zero Backlog project; computerization; and court-referred mediation

The record of recognition and donor support -- Filipino of the Year 2001, the Chief Justice's 2002 Ramon Magsaysay Award, the World Bank dinner, the Christchurch citation, CIDA's seven-million-dollar grant, USAID, ADB, UNDP and the European Commission -- offered as evidence that the APJR is 'not a hodgepodge of uncoordinated and poorly planned projects'

His closing appeal to the business audience: send opinions and support private-sector initiatives, report victimization by the CID plagues to the Chief Justice or Court Administrator, and above all 'never agree to bribe a judge directly or indirectly'
sub_topics: He thanks Rob Sears for the invitation to address 'this elite group representing American business' and notes that the judiciary has been in the news both for crucial decisions and for criticisms of how it reached them

Without going into personalities or specific litigations, he says the Court has long known its problems and has embarked on a comprehensive reform program, citing his own three books and several speeches on the subject
He names the three main problems -- corruption, incompetence and delay, 'the "CID" of our judicial system'

Corruption: at the May 3-5, 2002 political summit at the Manila Hotel there was a common sad perception of 'two types of law -- one for the rich and one for the poor,' with some judges believed to misinterpret the law for a price
He widens the definition beyond direct bribery to 'witchcraft, indecent proposals and bedeviling temptations' and the three 'ships': friendship, relationship and kinship

Incompetence: lawyers and judges whose poor command of language makes pleadings and decisions 'not only ungrammatical but also incomprehensible,' and jurists whose grasp of elementary law 'appalls even high school graduates'
Delay: antiquated procedures, rising case volume, many vacant judgeships, and litigants and lawyers who win 'by confusing, outwitting or bankrupting their opponents'

Discipline in the ranks: strict enforcement of the Canons of Judicial Ethics, and for the first time in its 100-year history the Court admonished one of its own members, dismissed a Court of Appeals justice, and suspended the Sandiganbayan's presiding magistrate from his administrative functions
Numbers as testament: from January 1, 1999 to April 9, 2002 the Court penalized about 350 erring lower-court judges with dismissals, suspensions, fines, reprimands and admonitions
Attracting talent: 33 percent of trial courts are vacant for lack of eligible applicants, leaving one judge for every 34,548 people, mainly because of inadequate pay

The pay figures: an RTC judge receives about P25,333 a month ('a measly $500'), CA and Sandiganbayan justices P27,500 and Supreme Court justices P38,500 -- a trial judge earning less than half what an equivalent lawyer in a progressive Makati firm makes, per a 1997 survey of 327 companies

Fiscal autonomy: the Constitution grants it but the political branches set the budget, the Salary Standardization Law governs pay, local-government support makes courts 'vulnerable to the wiles of local government officials,' and Congress has cut the judicial share from about two percent of the national budget in the early 90s to under one percent

The remedy sought: a fixed percentage of the national budget that the Court may allocate itself, plus exemption from the Salary Standardization Law, so judges' pay can rise by realignment without new funding

Continuing judicial education: Philja as the 'training school for justices, judges, court personnel, lawyers and aspirants to judicial posts,' whose courses no judicial nominee may skip; 92 training programs in 2001 reaching 2,673 judges, 3,901 personnel, 371 quasi-judicial officials and 172 aspirants
The proposed Philja Development Center on a three-hectare Tagaytay site, pursued with the Japan International Cooperation Agency

Rule-making and scholarship: updated Rules of Court, all-new Rules on Electronic Evidence, Corporate Rehabilitation, Intra-Corporate Controversies, Family Disputes, Intellectual Property and Juveniles in Conflict with the Law; a pending Bankers' Association proposal on restraining orders against foreclosures; and the Centenary Lecture Series on Shari'a, paperless courts, biotechnology, People Power and terrorism
The Benchbook for Judges and Benchbook on Penalties, funded by the Australian government and the Asia Foundation and now called 'the bibles of judges'

Zero Backlog: quality justice defined as 'not the rushing of kangaroo justice, but of justice based on truth,' with the Supreme Court's dormant cases cut from about 2,000 in 1995 to fewer than 50, the Court of Appeals following suit, but the lower courts worse -- RTC filings outstripping dispositions by about 6,800 a year and first-level courts by almost 65,000 a year over 1995-1999

Computerization: 1,500 personal computers purchased and distributed, loaded with Lex Libris containing decisions since 1901, the www.supremecourt.gov.ph homepage, computerized internal processes and case tracking, Manila terminals to watch trial-court calendars, and the year 2010 envisioned for 'paperless courts pioneered by countries like Singapore and Australia'

Alternative dispute resolution: Bouncing Checks Law cases form the bulk of lower-court dockets, so the Court promotes negotiation, arbitration and mediation as cheaper, speedier and less adversarial; about 400 mediators trained through Philja during the centenary, piloted on real cases in the NCR, Cebu and Davao in March-April 2001, with the Philippine Mediation Center established on April 6, 2001

Recognition and support: the Philippine Daily Inquirer's 'Filipino of the Year 2001' award, Social Weather Stations and Pulse Asia polling the Court as a trusted institution, and the Chief Justice's 2002 Ramon Magsaysay Award citing that 'as Chief Justice, he reformed the Philippine judiciary'

Donor backing: the World Bank country director hosting a July 5, 2000 dinner to recruit donors -- an inversion of the usual practice; the program cited at the 9th Conference of Chief Justices in Christchurch, October 4-8, 2001, making the Philippines 'a role model'; CIDA training, bridge financing and a seven-million-Canadian-dollar grant signed in Ottawa with Minister Susan Whelan; USAID training, communication strategy, mediation piloting and e-commerce expertise; ADB's independence study; UNDP's access proposal; a World Bank loan for six pilot 'e-courts'; and European Commission interest in judicial information sharing

The peroration: the reforms aim at 'a corps of competent, dedicated, honest and courageous judges' and at decisions that command public confidence even when 'unpalatable to current public sentiment,' creating 'stability in the rule of law and predictability in the rendition of decisions' as conditions of economic development

He quotes the Court's own line that leaders will be asked to account 'not only for what we did... but also for what visions we have today of our tomorrow,' then makes three requests of the audience -- send suggestions and support private-sector initiatives; report specific instances of corruption, incompetence or delay to the Office of the Chief Justice or the Court Administrator; and never consent to bribery, since 'corruption will take place only if litigants consent to or abet it' -- closing with 'Maraming salamat po'

stances.claim: The Philippine judiciary is beset by three main problems -- corruption, incompetence and delay, the 'CID' of the judicial system -- and the Court has long acknowledged them rather than denied them.
stances.rhetorical_move: candid self-diagnosis before defense: naming the plagues in an acronym and conceding public perception before describing the cure

stances.claim: Corruption is not only direct bribery; it is also 'the three "ships" that plague public service: friendship, relationship and kinship,' which compromise judges without money changing hands.
stances.rhetorical_move: definitional widening through an alliterative triad, converting a familiar word into a broader standard of conduct

stances.claim: The Court has matched words with unprecedented internal discipline -- for the first time in its 100-year history admonishing one of its own members, dismissing a Court of Appeals justice and suspending the Sandiganbayan's presiding magistrate, and penalizing about 350 lower-court judges between January 1999 and April 2002.
stances.rhetorical_move: proof by enumeration of firsts and counts, offered as 'not only as lip service... but also as testament'

stances.claim: Punishment alone cannot reform the judiciary; the Court must also 'entice the best and the brightest' with competitive pay, which requires a fixed share of the national budget and exemption from the Salary Standardization Law.
stances.rhetorical_move: argument from comparative figures -- peso and dollar salaries against a 1997 survey of 327 companies and a 33 percent trial-court vacancy rate

stances.claim: Quality justice means speed without sacrifice of truth -- 'not the rushing of kangaroo justice, but of justice based on truth; justice that is the product of a logic-driven process anchored on facts, law and reason.'
stances.rhetorical_move: definition-by-exclusion, ruling out the obvious misreading of a speed target before endorsing it

stances.claim: The APJR is 'not a hodgepodge of uncoordinated and poorly planned projects, but a sustained and widespread effort,' as shown by domestic honors and by donor bodies that sought the Court out rather than the reverse.
stances.rhetorical_move: external-validation close: awards, survey rankings, the World Bank hosting the donor dinner, and the Christchurch citation marshalled as third-party proof

stances.claim: Business has a duty in the fight: litigants must refuse bribery, since 'corruption will take place only if litigants consent to or abet it,' and 'while there are a few hoodlums in robes,' the majority of judges are honest and competent.
stances.rhetorical_move: three-part direct appeal to the audience, ending on a shared-responsibility claim paired with a defense of the bench's majority

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduces Artemio V. Panganiban's speech before 'this elite group representing American business in our country', delivered after weeks of criticism of how the judiciary had reached its recent decisions. Declining to discuss personalities or specific litigations, he said the Supreme Court had long recognized its problems and had embarked on the Action Program for Judicial Reform, begun in 2001 and due for full implementation by 2006. He named three: corruption, incompetence and delay -- 'the "CID" of our judicial system.' At the May 2002 political summit at the Manila Hotel, he reported, there was a common perception of 'two types of law -- one for the rich and one for the poor,' and corruption extends beyond bribery to 'the three "ships" that plague public service: friendship, relationship and kinship.' Incompetence showed in incomprehensible pleadings and in jurists whose grasp of elementary law 'appalls even high school graduates'; delay came from antiquated procedures, rising caseloads, vacant judgeships and litigants who win by 'confusing, outwitting or bankrupting their opponents.' On discipline, the Court had for the first time in its century admonished one of its own members, dismissed a Court of Appeals justice and suspended the Sandiganbayan's presiding magistrate, penalizing about 350 lower-court judges between January 1999 and April 2002. On recruitment, a third of trial courts stood vacant because a regional trial court judge earned about P25,333 -- 'a measly $500' -- less than half a comparable Makati lawyer's pay; the Court therefore sought a fixed share of the national budget, cut by Congress from two percent to under one, and exemption from the Salary Standardization Law. On competence, he cited Philja's 92 training programs in 2001, updated Rules of Court and new rules on electronic evidence, and the Benchbooks now called 'the bibles of judges.' On delay, he defined quality justice as 'not the rushing of kangaroo justice, but of justice based on truth,' reported that Zero Backlog had cut the Court's dormant cases from about 2,000 in 1995 to under 50 while lower-court filings still outran dispositions by thousands a year, described 1,500 computers loaded with Lex Libris, and promoted mediation. Domestic honors and donor support from the World Bank, CIDA, USAID and others, he said, proved that the APJR was 'not a hodgepodge of uncoordinated and poorly planned projects.' He closed by asking his audience for suggestions, for reports of wrongdoing to the Chief Justice or Court Administrator, and above all never to bribe a judge, since 'corruption will take place only if litigants consent to or abet it' -- assuring them that 'while there are a few hoodlums in robes,' the vast majority are 'men and women of integrity and competence.'
